WITH sl AS (SELECT sl.shipment_id, sum(sl.quantity*so.unit_price) po_val FROM erp_shipment_lines sl JOIN erp_so_lines so USING(line_id) GROUP BY 1),
b AS (SELECT i.customer_id, CAST(i.due_on AS DATE) due, CAST(p.paid_on AS DATE) paid, i.amount > sl.po_val*1.005 above FROM erp_invoices i JOIN erp_payments p USING(invoice_id) JOIN sl USING(shipment_id) WHERE i.invoiced_on<'2025-01-01' AND i.customer_id NOT IN (6,7)),
c AS (SELECT customer_id, count(*) FILTER (WHERE above) na, count(*) FILTER (WHERE NOT above) nm,
 avg(CASE WHEN paid-due>30 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) FILTER (WHERE above) ra, avg(CASE WHEN paid-due>30 THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) FILTER (WHERE NOT above) rm,
 median(paid-due) FILTER (WHERE above) mda, median(paid-due) FILTER (WHERE NOT above) mdm FROM b GROUP BY 1)
SELECT count(*) ncust, sum(na) n_above, sum(nm) n_match, round(sum(ra*na)/sum(na),4) r30_above_within, round(sum(rm*na)/sum(na),4) r30_match_reweighted, round(avg(CASE WHEN ra>rm THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END),4) share_cust_above_worse, round(median(mda-mdm),1) med_within_gap_days
FROM c WHERE na>=5 AND nm>=5

content.text:
I accepted the challenge, revised the finding and saved it as `finding.json` with `accepted: true`.

**What I accepted:**
1. **The "long tail" was really two things.** A share of it is a pricing problem, not slow payment:
   - Invoices billed above the customer's PO price are 7.32% of invoices but carry 22.67% of overdue dollar-days: $320,443 of the $1,413,693 in excess receivables (q181, q199, q211).
   - Outside customers 6 and 7, 65.28% of them are paid more than 30 days late, against 16.74% of correctly priced invoices.
2. **The 2022 peak wasn't purely a change in payment behaviour.** It combined a burst of above-PO invoices (27.93% of invoices outside customers 6 and 7 in 2022-H1) with a real but short slowdown on correctly priced ones: 9.29 to 17.78 days late, back to 10.49 by 2023-H1 (q200).
3. **The excess for customers 6 and 7 is smaller than I had it.** Measured on correctly priced invoices only, it is $247,935, or $19,835/yr at an assumed 8%, down from $270,734 (q199). I also dropped "consistent" for their payment lag: it is a wide spread (median 54–55 days to pay, only 3.4–3.6% on time), not a fixed payment cycle (q174, q175).

**My own test:** I checked whether the above-PO effect was just those invoices going to customers who pay late anyway (q221). It isn't. For the 99 customers outside 6 and 7 with both kinds of invoice:
- above-PO invoices are more than 30 days late 65.5% of the time, against 16.32% for the same customers' correctly priced invoices;
- 97.98% of those customers are worse on above-PO invoices;
- the median gap within a customer is 37 days.

**The revised finding:** excess receivables of $1,413,693, or $113,095/yr at the assumed 8% (cited to q199, which reproduces q139). The 2024 run-rate is similar. It splits into three parts that add up to the total:
- **Above-PO invoices: $320,443.** Interpretation, not confirmed: these look like invoices held until the price difference is settled, so the fix is agreeing prices before invoicing, not chasing payment. There are no dispute or hold records to prove it.
- **Customers 6 and 7, correctly priced invoices: $421,661.** They pay late every year and the cause is unknown; whether they have agreed terms other than net 30 still needs to be asked.
- **Everyone else's correctly priced invoices: $671,588.** 62.24% are paid within 5 days of due, with a second cluster at 31–90 days late spread across most customers. Nothing in the records explains it (not partial shipments, returns, late shipments or short payments). This is the only part a general collections process plausibly addresses.

The dollar figures are carrying costs at the assumed 8%, not cash lost, and only part of them is recoverable.
